SET CONTRACT (the engine depends on every line of it)
FORMAT

  the whole 2400 x 1350 canvas (overscan for camera pushes and pans); mid and near may stop at the frame edge.
- Three top-level groups in this order: <g id="far">, <g id="mid">, <g id="near">. Inside them, one named group per
  object (lowercase snake_case: table, chair_3, wall_screen, window_2). Draw the walls and the floor complete behind
  the furniture, so nothing has a hole when the layers slide apart.
- Light and surface effects go in classed groups inside each depth group: class="lm-shadow" (cast and contact
  shadows), class="lm-light" (light patches), class="lm-atmos" (haze, light shafts), class="lm-texture" (texture
  marks), class="lm-outline" (strokes, only if the style uses outlines), class="lm-hi" (highlight edges),
  class="lm-glow" (glow, only if the style uses it). Base shapes stay outside these groups.
- No <text>, no letters or numbers anywhere, no <image>, no filters, no masks, no clip paths, no external references.
  Gradients only where the style block allows them: two stops, palette colours only.
- Up to 700 KB per file; coordinates as integers or one decimal.

STYLE: PAINTERLY, GOUACHE IN VECTOR (for reflective, human and historical stories; wellbeing; values; moments that should feel felt)
- Paint the masses first: a clear value structure of light, middle and dark shapes, then colour with temperature shifts (warm light, cool shadow, warm bounce). Perspective is correct but drawn by hand, with no ruler-perfect edges.
- Edges are lost and found: some silhouettes dissolve into the wall behind them, others are crisp where the light hits; contours are shaped like brush strokes (tapered, slightly irregular paths), never a uniform outline.
- Gouache surface: flat, opaque strokes that follow the form, with a few dry-brush edges where a stroke runs out; detail is suggested by 2 or 3 strokes (the books on a shelf are a rhythm of coloured marks, not drawn books). Suggestion never removes structure: a chair still has its seat, back and legs in the right places.
- Simplify by distance: near objects get the most strokes, the far wall is a few broad planes.
- A limited palette per scene: at most five of the families carry the picture (the scene names them when it matters); the others appear only as small notes. Hard edges only at the focal point; edges soften toward the frame's sides. Keep each file under the size budget: fewer, larger brush strokes rather than many tiny ones.
- Light: Afternoon light painted as warm opaque strokes on surfaces it touches; shadows are cool and transparent-looking (shadow colour at 0.25 to 0.35 with brush-shaped edges); light spills and bounces (warm on the floor under the window, warm reflected light under the table edge). Direct low sun is warm; daylight that is only sky light (the room away from the sun patches) reads cool and slightly blue; lamps read orange. Keep those three apart.
- Texture: In lm-texture only, made of vector marks: brush streaks that follow surfaces (brick courses, wood grain, the weave of a rug), dry-brush flecks at stroke ends, a sparse paper grain. Dense where the light is, almost none in shadow. Never a noise overlay across the whole frame.
- Depth: Far: broad, softer, cooler, fewer strokes. Mid: full painting. Near: the boldest strokes and the warmest lights, a foreground object partly out of the frame.
- Quality bar: An illustrator's gouache painting for a thoughtful picture book or editorial cover for adults: you can feel the hand and the light, and the room still reads clearly at a glance.

- satellites: small boxy bodies with two flat solar panel wings and a few antennas, a few metres across; navigation satellites circle about 20,200 km up on six rings tilted 55 degrees to the equator, four or more per ring

- the Sun and planets: the real bodies at their real relative sizes and colours (NASA planetary fact sheet)

THE SET TO DRAW: earth_orbit: Earth seen from deep space with the 24 satellites of a satellite navigation constellation on their six tilted orbit rings around it, drawn at true scale, with the thin ring of low orbit hugging the planet and the far ring of geostationary orbit beyond (shots it serves: wide; used for how satellite navigation (GPS) finds a position, why timing from space matters to networks and payments, how far away satellites really are, space as infrastructure (weather, communications), space debris and sustainability)

Everything that has a size here is at that scale: the navigation satellites orbit at about 20,200 km above the surface (a ring radius of about 26,560 km from Earth's centre = 492 px); the crewed station's low orbit at about 420 km up (a ring radius of 126 px, only 8 px above the surface); geostationary orbit at about 35,786 km up (a ring radius of 781 px).
- The constellation (as the GPS baseline): 24 satellites, four on each of six orbit rings, each ring tilted 55 degrees to the equator and turned 60 degrees from the next around Earth's axis. The view looks at Earth from 18 degrees above the plane of its equator, so each ring shows as an ellipse.
- Satellites are a few metres across, far too small to see at this scale: each is drawn as a small symbol about 14 px wide, which the scene says is not to scale. The rings' ellipses below were computed from this geometry.

Hugging it, the low orbit is a fine pale ring 8 px outside the surface (an ellipse 252 by 78 px). The six navigation rings form a cage of ellipses around it, all 984 px long (half-axis 492 px) and centred on Earth: ring 1 tilted 145 degrees counterclockwise from horizontal, half-width 457 px; ring 2 at 122 degrees, half-width 187; ring 3 at 142 degrees, half-width 184; ring 4 at 15 degrees, half-width 283; ring 5 at 52 degrees, seen almost edge on (half-width 14); ring 6 at 57 degrees, half-width 358. Together they span about x 359 to 1321 and y 91 to 1029. Where a ring passes behind Earth it is hidden by the disc. ORDER
1. Work ONE set at a time. For each: write its short plan (horizon y, vanishing points, focal point, light direction and
   shadow direction, free zones for characters with their anchors, what goes in far, mid and near), draw it, run the
   quality check, fix, save its file. Only then start the next set.
2. Never reuse one set's geometry, camera or furniture layout for another: each follows its own brief.
3. Do not draw any variants until I approve the main sets.

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- airbrushed digital smoothness (perfect gradients, plastic sheen)
- a noise or grain overlay on everything
- uniform outlines
- every edge equally sharp
- muddy colour (shadows made by adding grey instead of shifting temperature)
- fiddly detail everywhere, or strident colours fighting each other
Not in this world:
- real agency logos, flags, mission patches, spacecraft names or real spacecraft drawn recognisably
- sci-fi: glowing corridors, holograms, laser beams, spaceships with fins
- planets or orbits at the wrong sizes when a scene says it is to scale
- sound waves, flames or smoke in space
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
